svg.title: Complication rates after thyroid surgery have no single denominator
svg.desc: Schematic on one subject: why the same complication is reported as two percentages that differ by a factor of ten. The figure runs in five parts. The first part draws the two headline ranges on one shared scale from zero to seventy per cent. All four bars are drawn as ranges with end caps; no median and no mean stands in for the span. The first bar is recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, reported at 2.3% to 26%, from a systematic review of 27 studies and about 25,000 patients. The reason block beside it explains that the same review gives mean rates of 9.8% for transient palsy and 2.3% for permanent palsy, while also stating that the reported rate runs from 2.3% all the way to 26% depending on how the larynx was examined; a tenfold spread whose source is not the operation but whether anyone went and looked. A tag underneath reads: the harder a unit looks, the worse its figures read. The second bar is hypoparathyroidism, reported in the literature at 0.5% to 65%, from a second systematic review of 45 studies and 23,164 patients. Its reason block records that the review opens with exactly this - incidence from 0.5% to 65%, mainly because each study defines it differently and above all because they differ on how many months separate transient from permanent - and that the same review recalculated both cutoffs on one consistent basis, giving permanent hypoparathyroidism of 4.11% on a six-month cutoff and 4.08% on a twelve-month cutoff, which is no difference at all, although that comparison holds only inside one analysis and not between separate studies. Its tag reads: comparable within one analysis, not across analyses. The third and fourth bars are the ranges the 2025 American Thyroid Association guidelines for differentiated thyroid cancer give for themselves: transient hypoparathyroidism 14% to 43% and permanent hypoparathyroidism 1% to 25%. The notes say that even the range printed in the guideline is a wide one, wide enough that it hardly looks like a medical figure, and that it is wide for the two reasons above; a twenty-five-fold span sits inside a single sentence, so when someone tells you that hypoparathyroidism after this operation runs at a certain percentage, the question to ask next is whether they mean transient or permanent, and how many months they are calling permanent. The second part is three cards that do have denominators, each read with its cohort. The first is a Scandinavian audit of 26 departments and 3,660 operations, mixing benign and malignant disease: unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy 3.9%, bilateral palsy 0.2%, still palsied at six months 0.97%, postoperative bleeding 2.1% and postoperative infection 1.6%, with an odds ratio of 8.18 for infection after nodal surgery, and, among the 1,648 bilateral procedures, hypocalcaemia needing active vitamin D in 9.9% at the first clinic visit and 4.4% at six months. This audit is also the source of the finding that routine laryngoscopy is itself an independent associated factor for unilateral vocal cord palsy, odds ratio 1.92. The second card is one high-volume surgeon with 2,527 nerves at risk and fibreoptic laryngoscopy before and after surgery in every patient: vocal fold motion impairment 2.9% and permanent impairment in 9 patients (0.4%), three of whom had the nerve deliberately divided during the operation because the cancer had invaded it. This is the lower end of the range under conditions where everybody is examined - what the left-hand end of the bar above actually looks like. The third card is a long-term voice survey of 308 respondents at a median of 10.7 years after surgery, with anyone carrying a recorded nerve injury deliberately excluded: 113 (37%) self-reported voice problems, but only 22 of them (7.1%) scored above the survey's abnormal cutoff. The commonest complaints were that the clarity of the voice is unpredictable at 23%, that people cannot hear them in a noisy place at 23%, and that they feel they have to strain to produce their voice at 21%. The card closes by saying that quoting only the 37% frightens people while quoting only the 7.1% leaves anyone with symptoms feeling they are making a fuss, and that the 2025 guideline text puts long-term voice change without nerve injury at over 30%. The third part shows how the extent of surgery changes the whole set. A meta-analysis gives relative risks for total thyroidectomy against lobectomy: transient hypocalcaemia 10.67 (95% confidence interval 5.75 to 19.31), permanent hypocalcaemia 3.17 (1.72 to 5.83), transient recurrent laryngeal nerve injury 1.69 (1.30 to 2.20), permanent nerve injury 1.85 (1.28 to 2.69) and postoperative bleeding 2.58 (1.69 to 3.93). A separate analysis of 62,722 operations uses overall complications instead, at 20.4% for total thyroidectomy against 10.8% for unilateral surgery. The endpoints here are hypocalcaemia and nerve injury themselves and the denominator is the studies included, not any one hospital. The fourth part draws the surgeon-volume threshold as three thresholds on three cards. Recommendation 6 of the 2025 American Thyroid Association guidelines gives more than 25 to 50 per year, a strong recommendation with moderate certainty, on the grounds that high-volume thyroid surgeons have on average fewer complications and better outcomes and that patients should be offered the option of referral to one, particularly for tumours needing more extensive surgery - and what it gives is a range, not a number. A 2017 national inpatient sample of 16,954 total thyroidectomies puts the inflection point at 26 per year, with a surgeon performing 1 case a year having 87% higher odds of a complication, 2 to 5 cases 68%, 6 to 10 cases 42%, 11 to 15 cases 22%, 16 to 20 cases 10% and 21 to 25 cases 3%. The United Kingdom registry of endocrine and thyroid surgery sees a decline only above 50 cases a year, with permanent hypoparathyroidism of 3% and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy of 2.6% in the highest-volume band of more than 100 a year, and its authors say the proportion of missing data is high and the figures may be biased. A note adds a 1998 analysis of 5,860 discharges from a single American state, where the highest-volume group had 5.1% inpatient complications, the middle two 6.1% and the lowest-volume group 8.6%, and where complications and length of stay depended on the surgeon's experience with no consistent association for hospital volume. A yellow banner reads "26, 50, 100 - three thresholds, one question with no agreed answer", and says that folding those three numbers into one sentence about a minimum annual caseload is not something to do, because they come from different databases, different eras and different definitions of complication. The fifth part answers why the blood tests for calcium keep coming. The 2018 statement devoted to postoperative hypoparathyroidism defines it as a low parathyroid hormone level together with a low calcium level, both at once; a postoperative parathyroid hormone below 15 pg/mL indicates a raised risk of acute hypoparathyroidism; and the same statement lists the risk factors as bilateral surgery, autoimmune thyroid disease, central neck dissection, retrosternal goitre, limited surgical experience and malabsorption. Recommendation 24B of the 2025 guideline says that after total thyroidectomy or central neck dissection calcium and vitamin D should be given according to the parathyroid hormone level, which reduces hypocalcaemia and shortens hospital stay better than observation with serial calcium measurements alone; strong recommendation, moderate certainty. The figure ends with a red-bordered block headed "This figure does not give you a percentage you can use to compare hospitals", holding four statements. Every reported rate has to carry how it was looked for and how it was defined, and without either one two hospitals' figures stop being comparable. The two Swedish papers are cohorts of people operated on for benign thyroid disease rather than cancer: of 4,899 patients, 246 (5.2%) had permanent hypoparathyroidism and over a mean follow-up of 4.4 years the adjusted mortality hazard ratio was 2.09 (95% confidence interval 1.04 to 4.20), while a second paper from the same registry of 4,828 patients gives 4.88 (2.00 to 11.95) for renal insufficiency and 1.88 (1.02 to 3.47) for cardiovascular events in those with pre-existing cardiovascular disease; those numbers are not carried across to cancer, and what they do say is that permanent hypoparathyroidism is not a trivial thing. The figure gives no dose and no duration for calcium tablets or active vitamin D, which follow the protocol of the operating hospital, and the 2025 guideline makes preoperative voice assessment a strong recommendation with moderate certainty. Finally, two sentences to read out at the preoperative clinic - do you scope every patient after surgery or only those with symptoms, and how many months on active vitamin D do you count as permanent - and two numbers to ask for on the day of discharge: what is my calcium today, and what is my parathyroid hormone.

g.text: ONE PERCENTAGE, NO SINGLE DENOMINATOR
This number has no
single denominator: two
ranges, and what makes
them
For the same complication you will find 2% written in
one place and more than 20% in another. Nobody is
lying to you, and no hospital is unusually bad. The
reported rate depends on two things: how it was
looked for, and how it was defined.
So this figure draws them as ranges, and puts the
reason for each range beside it. A percentage quoted
on its own, without its method of ascertainment and its
definition, tells you almost nothing.
Two ranges, and what makes them
One shared scale, from zero to seventy per cent. All four are drawn as
ranges with end caps: no median, no mean, no single good-looking number
standing in for the whole span.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy: reported at 2.3% to
A systematic review of 27 studies and about 25,000 patients
Where the range comes from: whether every patient had a
laryngoscopy
The same review gives mean rates of 9.8% for transient palsy
and 2.3% for permanent palsy. It also states that the reported
rate runs all the way from 2.3% to 26% depending on how the
larynx was examined.
A tenfold spread, and its source is not the operation. It is
whether anyone went and looked.
The harder a unit looks, the worse its figures read
Hypoparathyroidism: reported in the literature at
A second systematic review, of 45 studies and 23,164 patients
Where the range comes from: the definition, and the cutoff
between transient and permanent
The review opens with exactly this: reported incidence runs
from 0.5% to 65%, mainly because each study defines it
differently, and above all because they differ on how many
months separate transient from permanent.
That same review recalculated both cutoffs on one consistent
basis: permanent hypoparathyroidism is 4.11% on a six-month
cutoff and 4.08% on a twelve-month cutoff, which is no
difference at all. But that comparison holds inside one analysis.
Between separate studies it still does not hold.
Comparable within one analysis, not across analyses
The range the 2025 guideline gives itself: transient
hypoparathyroidism 14% to 43%
2025 American Thyroid Association guidelines for differentiated thyroid
cancer
Even the range printed in the guideline is a wide one
Wide enough that it hardly looks like a medical figure - and it is
wide for the two reasons above.
The range the 2025 guideline gives itself: permanent
hypoparathyroidism 1% to 25%
The same guideline, the same passage
A twenty-five-fold span, written inside one sentence
So when someone tells you that hypoparathyroidism after this
operation runs at a certain percentage, the question to ask next
is: transient or permanent, and how many months are you
calling permanent?
The figures that do have a denominator,
read together with their cohort
Each of the three cards below has a stated denominator and a stated
method. They can be quoted - but only together with the line in brackets.
A Scandinavian audit: 26 departments, 3,660
operations
(A surgical audit mixing benign and malignant disease)

palsy
Bilateral palsy
Still palsied at six months

Postoperative infection

This is also the source of the finding that routine laryngoscopy is

(Fibreoptic laryngoscopy before and after surgery in every patient)
Vocal fold motion impairment
Permanent (9 patients)
Three of those 9 had the nerve deliberately divided during the
operation because the cancer had invaded it.
This is the lower end of the range under conditions where

(Patients with any recorded nerve injury were deliberately excluded)

people)
The commonest complaints were "the clarity of my voice is
unpredictable" at 23%, "people cannot hear me in a noisy place" at
23%, and "I feel I have to strain to produce my voice" at 21%.
Quoting only the 37% frightens people; quoting only the 7.1% leaves
anyone with symptoms feeling they are making a fuss. The 2025

How much is removed changes the whole
set
A meta-analysis gives relative risks for total thyroidectomy against

themselves, and the denominator is the studies that were included - not
any one hospital.
Transient hypocalcaemia
10.67 (95% confidence interval 5.75 to 19.31)
Permanent hypocalcaemia

Permanent recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
Postoperative bleeding
A separate analysis of 62,722 operations uses overall

for unilateral surgery. The direction is stable, but this too is a

The surgeon-volume threshold is not one
number either
Three databases produce three thresholds. Nobody has miscalculated.
There simply is no consensus on what counts as high volume.
2025 American Thyroid Association guidelines, Recommendation 6
More than 25 to 50 per year
Because high-volume thyroid surgeons have on average fewer
complications and better outcomes, patients with thyroid cancer
should be offered the option of referral to a high-volume surgeon,
particularly for tumours needing more extensive surgery. Strong
recommendation, moderate certainty. Note that what it gives is a
range, not a number.
A 2017 national inpatient sample of 16,954 total thyroidectomies

A surgeon performing 1 case a year has 87% higher odds of a
complication; 2 to 5 cases, 68%; 6 to 10, 42%; 11 to 15, 22%; 16 to 20,
The United Kingdom registry of endocrine and thyroid surgery
(UKRETS)
More than 50 per year
In this registry the decline only appears above 50 cases a year; in
the highest-volume band, more than 100 a year, permanent
hypoparathyroidism is 3% and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy 2.6%.
The authors say themselves that the proportion of missing data is
high and the figures may be biased.
And a 1998 analysis of 5,860 discharges from a single American state: the
highest-volume group had 5.1% inpatient complications, the middle two 6.1%, and
the lowest-volume group 8.6%; complications and length of stay depended on the
surgeon's experience, with no consistent association for hospital volume.
26, 50, 100 - three thresholds, one
question with no agreed answer
Folding those three numbers into one sentence about a
minimum annual caseload is not something to do. They come
from different databases, different eras and different
definitions of complication.
So why the repeated blood tests for
calcium
The definition first: two conditions have to hold at once
The 2018 statement devoted to postoperative
hypoparathyroidism puts it plainly: it means a low
parathyroid hormone level together with a low calcium level.
Both, at the same time.
A postoperative parathyroid hormone below 15 pg/mL
indicates a raised risk of acute hypoparathyroidism. The
same statement lists the risk factors: bilateral surgery,
autoimmune thyroid disease, central neck dissection,
retrosternal goitre, limited surgical experience and
malabsorption.
Recommendation 24B of the 2025 guideline: after total
thyroidectomy or central neck dissection, calcium and
vitamin D should be given according to the parathyroid
hormone level, which reduces hypocalcaemia and shortens
hospital stay better than observation with serial calcium
measurements alone. Strong recommendation, moderate
certainty.
This figure does not give you a percentage you can
use to compare hospitals
Every reported rate has to carry two things: how it was
looked for (was every patient scoped after surgery, or only
those with symptoms), and how it was defined (how many
months on active vitamin D before it is called permanent).
Drop either one and two hospitals' figures stop being
comparable.
The two Swedish papers are cohorts of people who had a
total thyroidectomy FOR BENIGN THYROID DISEASE, not for
cancer: of 4,899 patients, 246 (5.2%) had permanent
hypoparathyroidism, and over a mean follow-up of 4.4 years
the adjusted mortality hazard ratio was 2.09 (95% confidence
interval 1.04 to 4.20); a second paper from the same
registry, of 4,828 patients, gives a hazard ratio of 4.88 (2.00
to 11.95) for renal insufficiency and 1.88 (1.02 to 3.47) for
cardiovascular events in those with pre-existing
cardiovascular disease. Those numbers are not carried
across to cancer. What they do say is that permanent
hypoparathyroidism is not a trivial thing.
This figure gives no dose and no duration for calcium tablets
or active vitamin D; that follows the postoperative protocol
of the hospital where you are operated on. The 2025
guideline also makes preoperative voice assessment a
strong recommendation with moderate certainty - your
voice recorded before the operation is the only thing there
will be to compare against afterwards.
Two sentences to read out at the preoperative clinic: "Do
you scope every patient after surgery, or only the ones with
symptoms?" and "How many months on active vitamin D do
you count as permanent?" Then, on the day you are
discharged, two numbers: what is my calcium today, and
what is my parathyroid hormone.
Schematic, redrawn from the 2009 systematic review of the
diagnosis of recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy after thyroidectomy,
the 2008 Scandinavian multicentre surgical audit, the 2021
systematic review of hypoparathyroidism definitions, the 2025
American Thyroid Association guidelines for differentiated thyroid
cancer and the 2018 ATA statement on postoperative
hypoparathyroidism, the 2018 single high-volume surgeon
laryngoscopy series, the 2013 hemithyroidectomy meta-analysis, the
2021 long-term voice survey, the 1998 and 2017 surgeon-volume
analyses, the United Kingdom registry of endocrine and thyroid
surgery and the 2014 analysis of complications after total
thyroidectomy; not reproduced from the figures of the original
papers. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies
differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
